catalog_quote: [3.6] There is no rigorous phonological difference between clitics, suffixes, and postposed particles such as postpositions. Stress and accent patterns, which in other languages of the world often bring out cliticization, are not relevant to Nanga. ... [2.1] Nanga has a typical Dogon stem-level tonal system, with at least one (lexical) high tone element per stem. At the level of syllables, tones are H[igh], L[ow], <HL> (falling), <LH> (rising), and bell-shaped <LHL>. There are no <HLH> syllables. ... Verb stems are lexically /LH/ or /H/. ... Several suffixes impose specific tone overlays on the preceding stem, overriding lexical tones. ... [3.2.2] Segmental phonological rules generally point to a trochaic bias, i.e. bisyllabic [sw] with a strong followed by a weak. tone_statements.quote: In eastern Dogon languages, the typical situation is that verbs are either lexically /H/ or /LH/. ... The /LH/ melody on trisyllabics is realized as Cv̀.Cv̀.Cv́ (L.L.H) or as Cv̀.Cv́.Cv́ (L.H.H) depending on the language, as shown in (2). (2) a. L.L.H eastern: Toro Tegu, Jamsay, Ben Tey, Donno So ... b. L.H.H (s.t. varying with L.H.L) eastern: Nanga, Bankan Tey, Togo Kan northwestern: Najamba ... In eastern Dogon languages, typical lexical melodies for uncompounded stems other than verbs are /H/, /HL/, /LH/, and /LHL/. ... Possible examples of /HLH/ in Nanga and Ben Tey might be analysed as compounds. ... Nanga appears to have relexified *Cv́Cv̀ as Cv́Cv̂, with final falling tone.

tone_statements.quote: Lastly, in Nanga, tonal assignment is variable. One possible surface form is for the hierarchically lower cophonology, associated with the possessor, to prevail (McPherson 2014:74). Another possible surface form shows the modifier's tonal assignment dominating, such that both the possessor and noun surface with a low tone, as in Jamsay (McPherson 2014:149).

tone_statements.summary: When a possessor and an adjective both target the noun in Nanga, either the possessor's H(L) overlay or the adjective's L overlay can win, so the same phrase has more than one surface tone pattern. Secondary data (McPherson 2014); the authors note that real frequency data are unavailable, so the 0.6/0.4 observed values in their tableau are adopted, not counted.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura & Jeffrey Heath. 2016. Phrasal grammatical tone in the Dogon languages: The role of constraint interaction. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 34(2): 593-639.
tone_statements.quote: (17c) PossIP HL N Adj (Nanga) / ú lésî mÒsí / 2sg.pro uncle ugly / 'your ugly uncle' (cf. lèsí) [p. 18]. "In Nanga, the lower controller, i.e. the possessor, takes precedence and imposes {HL} on the possessed noun; the adjective's {L} overlay goes unrealized. As a first approximation, we can say that in Tommo So and Jamsay, a constraint motivating the adjective's tonal overlay outranks the possessor's (Adjective ≫ Possessor), while in Nanga, the reverse is true (Possessor ≫ Adjective)" [p. 19]. General: "Like all Dogon languages, it has a phonemic distinction between L and H tone" and "almost all Dogon languages have a ban on lexically /L/ words" [p. 5]; "Every Dogon language studied to date has a tonosyntactic system" [p. 53].
tone_statements.locator: manuscript pp. 18-19; general Dogon statements pp. 5 and 53

tone_statements.summary: Nanga definites, which grew out of demonstratives, keep their power to tone-lower the preceding noun, unlike Najamba definites. Postnominal pronominal possessors put {HL} on a resumptive classifier ([ú HLyɛ̂]) rather than on the noun.

audit.reasoning: The classification 'tonal, no stress rule' rests on the only existing description of Nanga, a 444-page 2016 reference grammar by the language's sole documenter, which we hold and whose deciding sentences ('Stress and accent patterns.. are not relevant to Nanga'; 'typical Dogon stem-level tonal system'; 'trochaic bias' from segmental rules only) are confirmed verbatim at the cited pages. Glottolog lists no other descriptive work; web search turned up only tonosyntax studies (McPherson 2014 diss., downloaded; McPherson & Heath 2016 NLLT) that reuse Heath's data and are silent on word stress. Nothing better exists and nothing suggests the classification is wrong.

sources.citation: McPherson, Laura E. 2014. Replacive grammatical tone in the Dogon languages. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles. 370 pp.
sources.quote: Treats Nanga as a lexical+replacive grammatical tone language ('Nanga is one of the most tonosyntactically complex languages in the sample', p. 163); data explicitly from Heath's grammar drafts. No statement on Nanga word stress; the only 'stress' discussion (sec. 2.7.2, p. 118) is a diachronic speculation that Dogon tonal overlays originated in phrasal de-emphasis, not a synchronic stress claim.

Nanga) are lexically /H/ or /LH/, melody largely predictable from initial obstruent voicing; Nanga is a 'left-edge tone break' language (trisyllabic /LH/ = L.H.H, sometimes varying with L.H.L), grouped with Bankan Tey and Togo Kan; Nanga 'bring' jě: /LH/ regular; non-verb stems have melodies /H/, /HL/, /LH/, /LHL/ (no lexical /L/, /HLH/ marginal -- possible Nanga /HLH/ items analysable as compounds); Nanga has relexified *Cv́Cv̀ as Cv́Cv̂ with final falling tone; syllable tones H, L, <HL>, <LH>, occasionally <LHL>; grammatical overlays erase lexical melodies.
